scope: One match ISR vs BRA (2 sets, 60 scoreboard points, cleaned broadcast video timebase, 25 fps), repo tomerzi/fotevolley commit 64c0e79. Exploratory single-match analysis; no video was available for visual verification.

findings.title: ISR conversion after losing a point collapsed in set 2
findings.hypothesis: ISR's ability to win the next point after conceding (side-out under the winner-serves rule) differs between sets
findings.comparison: ISR points won immediately after BRA won the previous point: set 1 vs set 2; plus BRA reference
findings.effect: ISR 10/17 (59%) in set 1 vs 5/17 (29%) in set 2, -29 percentage points; BRA 10/13 (77%) vs 5/11 (45%). In set 2 BRA had runs of 5 (points 32-36) and 9 (points 39-47). ISR also won only 9/24 (38%) points right after winning one, vs BRA 19/34 (56%).
findings.interpretation: The scoreboard sequence is verified. The decisive gap is ISR's inability to stop BRA runs in set 2 and to keep a point after winning one. Under the standard rally-scoring rule (point winner serves) this means ISR's receive phase failed in set 2 and ISR's serve gave little advantage, but serve identity was not observed in the data.
findings.limitations: Only 2 sets; consecutive points are serially dependent so rates have wide uncertainty (17 opportunities per set). Serve team is a rule assumption; rally windows could not be aligned to serves. No information on why points were lost (errors vs opponent winners).
findings.counterexample: ISR closed set 2 with streaks of 4 (points 50-53) and 3 (55-57), so the set-2 collapse is concentrated in points 32-47, not uniform.
findings.practice_drill: Pressure side-out game: coach serves to ISR repeatedly; ISR must win 2 consecutive rallies after any lost rally to score; track receive-to-attack success per block of 10.
findings.follow_up_measure: Next match: ISR win rate on the point after conceding (target >= 50% in every set), plus manual serve labels to confirm receive vs serve split.

sources.selection: all 60 points; first point of each set has no previous winner

findings.title: Fixed left/right roles in both pairs; ISR shape more variable and shifted to the left
findings.hypothesis: The two pairs use different defensive formations when the ball crosses into their half
findings.unit: incoming ball crossing (pair snapshot), clustered by rally
findings.comparison: ISR vs BRA pair geometry at the frame the ball crosses the net into their half; player occupancy during active play
findings.effect: Left-side player fixed: ISR_B left in 62/64 snapshots, BRA_B in 64/64. ISR_A was the deeper partner in 43/64 (67%) vs BRA balanced 36/28. Separation median ISR 3.58 m (IQR 3.01-3.94) vs BRA 3.21 m (3.02-3.47); depth stagger IQR ISR 0.40-1.81 m vs BRA 0.48-1.00 m. ISR_B spent 64% of active frames in the left third (team view); ISR_A 69% in the centre third and only 26% in the right third, whereas BRA_A spent 51% in the right third.
findings.interpretation: Both teams keep specialised sides. BRA holds a compact, nearly side-by-side shape around 3.0-3.5 m. ISR alternates between side-by-side and a front/back split with ISR_A deep, and as a pair sits left of centre, leaving the right channel (team view) to a centrally positioned ISR_A.
findings.limitations: Positions use bounding-box feet through a homography with no landmark residuals; airborne players are mis-projected. 99.5% of boxes are not manually verified. Anchor is the ball crossing frame, not the opponent contact. Occupancy describes positioning, not success. Descriptive only.
findings.counterexample: In 21/64 ISR snapshots ISR_B was the deeper player, so the front/back split is a tendency, not a fixed rule; ISR stagger <2 m in 29/39 labelled events.
findings.practice_drill: Shadow-defence drill: coach signals opponent attack from three zones; ISR pair must arrive in a pre-agreed side-by-side base (3.0-3.5 m apart, both 4-5 m from net) before the signal; ISR_A rehearses covering the right channel.
findings.follow_up_measure: Next match: share of ISR incoming snapshots with separation 3.0-3.5 m and stagger <1 m, and ISR_A right-third occupancy.

sources.selection: non-interpolated boxes; anchor frames from ball crossings and frames inside possession runs

findings.title: ISR lost most incoming balls when caught >= 4 m apart at the crossing - but only at the crossing moment
findings.hypothesis: Wide partner separation when the opponent's ball crosses the net is associated with failing to return it
findings.comparison: Failed defence (rally ended on their half and they lost) vs returned, by separation >= 4 m vs < 4 m at the crossing frame
findings.effect: ISR: 6/8 (75%) failed when >= 4 m vs 3/31 (10%) when < 4 m; rally-bootstrap difference (both teams) +50 pp, 95% CI 17-79 pp. Rally level: 6/7 ISR rallies containing a wide crossing ended in failed defence vs 3/23 others. BRA was almost never >= 4 m apart (2/39). Modeled coverage (coverage.py, 4 scenarios, R 2.65-5.27 m) showed no difference in uncovered area between failed and returned balls.
findings.interpretation: Separation at the crossing is more likely a symptom of being pulled apart (one partner already chasing, blocking or out of position after the previous attack) than a chosen formation: measured 0.2 s earlier the association disappears (2/8 vs 7/31). The coaching-relevant question is transition: how ISR recovers into a connected shape after its own attack.
findings.limitations: Outcome label depends on unverified scoreboard-to-play alignment; 33 unclean and 10 terminal_won possessions excluded; 8 wide events in 7 rallies; anchor sensitivity fails; feet projection wrong during jumps; threshold 4 m chosen from a 3-split predeclared grid (6 tests). No video check.
findings.counterexample: s1_p3 (frame 442) and s1_p27 (frame 5543): ISR >= 4 m apart and still returned the ball. Three ISR failures occurred with separation 2.3-3.8 m.
findings.practice_drill: Attack-and-recover drill: ISR attacks a fed ball, coach immediately counter-attacks; pair must close to <= 3.5 m and both be 3-5 m from net before the counter-ball crosses; score only rallies where the recovery shape is reached.
findings.follow_up_measure: After manual serve/contact labels: ISR separation at the opponent's attack contact (not the crossing), and failed-defence rate by recovery shape; check if the effect replicates in a second match.
findings.model_assumptions: coverage.py isotropic reach on a 9x9 m half, 30x30 grid, reaction 0.25 s, base reach 1.0 m, horizons 0.8/1.2 s, speeds 3/4.5 m/s; ground-plane only, ignores ball trajectory and jumps.

findings.title: BRA control the first touch with the foot twice as often as ISR; foot first touches led to a full 3-touch build-up more often
findings.hypothesis: Teams differ in the body region used for ball control, and the first-touch region is linked to the possession structure that follows
findings.comparison: Share of foot contacts BRA vs ISR (all candidates and first touch of a possession); 3-touch build-up rate and opponent outcome by first-touch region
findings.effect: Foot share of all keypoint-matched candidates: BRA 32/110 (29%) vs ISR 18/110 (16%), +13 pp, rally-bootstrap 95% CI +0.6 to +24 pp, 53 rallies. Same direction on both screen halves (BRA 17/60 and 15/50; ISR 7/52 and 11/58) and in both sets. First touch: BRA foot 23/54 (43%) vs ISR 13/58 (22%); ISR chest 16/58 (28%) vs BRA 8/54 (15%). First touch with the foot reached >=3 candidate touches in 14/36 (39%) possessions vs 8/41 (20%) after a head first touch.
findings.interpretation: BRA appear to absorb the incoming ball with the foot and then build a full three-touch possession; ISR take more first balls on the chest or head and play more directly. This is a measurable difference in control style, but there is no evidence here that it produces better attacks.
findings.limitations: Contacts are inferred from the 2D ball path (lowest point and vertical reversal) and the nearest 2D pose keypoint within 15% of box height; no contact was visually verified. Low balls near the sand are missed more often, which biases all teams toward head contacts. Pose was run on an older box set (99.3% of necks fall inside v9 boxes). Body region is coarse; foot surface is not identifiable. 61 candidates excluded (no keypoint within 15% of box height).
findings.counterexample: After a foot first touch the opponent failed to return the resulting attack 0/15 times (labelled), vs 4/24 after a head first touch, so the fuller build-up did not translate into more opponent failures in this match.
findings.practice_drill: ISR first-touch drill: coach feeds mid-height balls to each ISR player; the receiver must control with the foot to a 1 m target zone in front of the partner, then the pair completes a 3-touch attack. Score successful foot controls out of 20 per player.
findings.follow_up_measure: With manual contact labels: per-player first-touch region share, controllable-reception rate by region, and set quality after foot vs chest receptions in the next match.
